opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. You know, if you look around you, almost every big problem we face as a society eventually comes down to materials. Think about climate change: we need better batteries to store renewable energy, better catalysts to make fertilizer or fuels without burning so much natural gas, materials that can capture carbon dioxide directly from the air. Think about semiconductors, the chips that run all of our AI, or solar panels, or even something as basic as cement and steel, which are huge contributors to emissions. All of these are materials problems at their core.

And the interesting thing is that the space of possible materials is astronomically large. You can combine elements of the periodic table in so many ways, with different structures and different processing conditions, that humans have really only explored a tiny corner of it. Historically, discovering a new material has been slow, often a mix of intuition, trial and error, and a fair bit of luck. It can take ten or twenty years to go from discovery to something that's actually deployed.

That's exactly where I think AI can make a dramatic difference. We now have the ability to learn surrogate models that approximate quantum mechanical simulations, like density functional theory, orders of magnitude faster. We have generative models that can propose new candidate structures rather than just screening a fixed list. And if you couple that with automated, robotic labs, you can start to close the loop: the model proposes, the lab synthesizes and measures, the data flows back, and the model improves. That kind of active learning loop could compress the discovery timeline enormously.

There's also a nice property of materials compared to, say, drug discovery. In drug discovery, a lot of the bottleneck is clinical trials, which are slow, expensive, and involve human biology that we don't fully understand. In materials, the physics is, in a sense, more tractable. The equations are known, Schrödinger's equation, and the experiments are often faster and cheaper to run. So the feedback loop can be much tighter, which is exactly what machine learning thrives on.

So for me, it's this combination: enormous societal impact, a huge unexplored search space, and a problem structure that's really well suited to modern AI. And honestly, as someone who started out in physics, it feels a bit like coming home, using these tools to go back and tackle fundamental physical problems that really matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, if you think about it, almost everything we care about in terms of the big problems of our time comes down to materials in one way or another. Take climate change. If you want to capture carbon out of the atmosphere, you need a material that does that efficiently. If you want better batteries so we can actually electrify transportation and store renewable energy, that's a materials problem. Solar cells, catalysts to make green hydrogen, fertilizer that doesn't require the enormous energy of the Haber-Bosch process, superconductors, better chips — all of these are, at the bottom, questions of finding the right arrangement of atoms with the right properties.

And the thing that makes this exciting to me is that the search space is essentially infinite. The number of possible stable compounds you can make is astronomically large, and we've explored only a tiny, tiny corner of it. Historically, the way we found new materials was largely trial and error, with a lot of human intuition and a lot of luck. The lithium-ion battery took decades. So if you can accelerate that loop, even by a factor of ten, the implications are enormous.

Now, why AI? The reason is that in principle we know the physics. The Schrödinger equation tells you, given the atoms, what the properties are. The problem is that solving it exactly is intractable, and even the approximations we use, like density functional theory, are very expensive. So you have this beautiful situation where you have a well-defined simulator that is too slow, and machine learning is extremely good at learning fast surrogates of slow simulators. You generate data with the expensive method, you train a neural network that respects the symmetries of the problem — rotations, translations, permutations of identical atoms — and now you have something that's orders of magnitude faster. And once you have that, you can do things that were previously unthinkable: screen millions of candidates, run long molecular dynamics simulations, do generative design where you go backwards from the property you want to the structure that gives it to you.

I also think materials is, in a sense, a more tractable place to start than something like biology. In biology you have this enormous complexity of the cell, of the organism, and the data is noisy and hard to collect. In materials, the physics is cleaner, the simulations are more trustworthy, and increasingly we have automated labs that can actually synthesize and test what the model proposes. So you can close the loop between hypothesis and experiment much faster.

And I'll say one more thing. I spent a lot of my career on fundamental machine learning — Bayesian methods, variational inference, equivariant networks. At some point you ask yourself, what do I actually want to do with this? And for me the answer was that I want to use it to solve real problems, and materials is where I see the most direct path from better models to a better world. That's really why I moved in this direction.

astra-6.text:
Well, materials are at the heart of so many of the problems we need to solve. If you want better batteries, cheaper solar cells, or more efficient ways to capture carbon, you’re often looking for a material with particular properties. A discovery at that level can have consequences across an entire industry.

The challenge is that the space of possible materials is enormous. You can’t simply make everything in a lab and see what works, and even simulating all those possibilities is far too expensive. AI gives us a way to explore that space more intelligently: to predict properties, identify promising candidates, and guide the next experiment.

And ultimately, you’d like to turn the problem around. Instead of asking, ‘What does this material do?’ you ask, ‘What material would give me the properties I need?’ You still have to establish that you can actually synthesize it and that it works in practice. But that connection between computation and something physical, something that could help solve an energy or climate problem, is what makes this so exciting.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you think about the challenges we face—energy, climate, sustainability—many of them come down to materials. We need better batteries, better catalysts, better ways to capture carbon, and ways to produce things like steel and cement with much less energy. A new material can change what’s possible in any of those areas.

The difficulty is that the space of possible materials is enormous. You can vary the elements, their composition, their structure, and how you manufacture them. We can’t explore all of that by trial and error in a laboratory, and even accurate computer simulations can be very expensive.

That’s where AI becomes interesting. It can help us predict properties much faster and guide us toward promising candidates. Ultimately, you’d like to work backwards: specify the properties you need and use a model to propose materials, then test them and learn from those experiments. That connection between computation and the physical world is what makes this such an exciting opportunity.
